text: Input-side control is not new: prosodic symbols in the input sequence were routine in unit-selection and hidden Markov model (HMM) TTS, and Kurihara \emph{et al.}~\cite{kurihara2021prosodic} carried them into neural sequence-to-sequence TTS. UtterTune~\cite{kato2025uttertune} realizes them for a modern LLM-based backbone by wrapping the target word in two special tokens carrying an accented katakana reading. Sarashina2.2-TTS~\cite{sarashina2026tts} describes the same family of mechanisms (Sec.~3.2.1 of that report). Mixing phoneme or reading input into the training set --- CosyVoice~3's pronunciation inpainting~\cite{du2025cosyvoice3}, GLM-TTS's hybrid phoneme--text input~\cite{cui2025glmtts} --- gives control only where the base was trained with it. Training-free editing exists for released models: SonoEdit~\cite{singh2026sonoedit} rewrites one word's pronunciation in an LLM-based TTS by a closed-form weight edit, and FlowEdit~\cite{singh2026flowedit} stores a correction as a text-embedding perturbation in a flow-matching TTS; both correct one word at a time from a supplied exemplar (a synthesis from an International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcription, or a native recording) and address segmental pronunciation, not accent. What is unresolved for a released model is the \emph{cost} of installing the channel afterward

What is unresolved for a released model is the \emph{cost} of installing the channel afterward and its \emph{reach}. Both published instances of the tag channel pay in recorded speech: $15{,}097$ hand-corrected JSUT/JVS~\cite{sonobe2017jsut,takamichi2019jvs} pairs in UtterTune, ${\approx}4{,}000$\,h of supervised fine-tuning in Sarashina2.2-TTS, a capability not included in the released weights.

This paper removes the recording cost entirely. Given a reading spelled out, the model can already say it; what it lacks is a channel that carries the reading and the accent together, and we install that channel by distilling the model against itself. What is new is the training pair, not the adapter or the tag.

Given a reading spelled out, the model can already say it; what it lacks is a channel that carries the reading and the accent together, and we install that channel by distilling the model against itself. What is new is the training pair, not the adapter or the tag.

\noindent\textbf{Contributions.}
(i) A self-distillation procedure that installs reading and accent control into a frozen TTS backbone using no recorded speech, no human labels, and no corpus --- only a text set and a public front-end (\S\ref{sec:method}).
(ii) Evidence, from screened raters, that it gives an accent notation a meaning the base never had: on Sarashina2.2-TTS, the tag realizes the prescribed accent on $0.89$ of unseen words against $0.57$ for plain kana, with kana winning no pair, at no measurable naturalness cost (\S\ref{sec:exp}).
(iii) The deployment form that makes it usable: register a word once, and every later occurrence is corrected automatically, accent included (\S\ref{sec:deploy}).
(iv) A transfer test: the same recipe moved untuned to three other backbones transfers reading on all three and accent in part on CosyVoice~2 but not on Irodori, and naturalness on none yet; Table~\ref{tab:summary} lays this out, and the reasons are located (\S\ref{sec:reftab}, \S\ref{sec:nat}).

\subsection{Self-distilled teachers}
Let $w$ be a \emph{common} word that the base pronounces correctly, and $c(w)$ be a natural carrier sentence containing $w$ in ordinary orthography. We synthesize $c(w)$ with the frozen base and keep \emph{its own output} as the target. The student input $\tilde c(w)$ is $c(w)$ with $w$ replaced by its tagged accented reading. Distilling
\[
\tilde c(w) \;\longmapsto\; \text{base output for } c(w)
\]

\[
\tilde c(w) \;\longmapsto\; \text{base output for } c(w)
\]
teaches the model to honor an explicit reading and accent instruction while changing nothing else, because the teacher and the student describe the same utterance. No recording, annotation, or corpus is involved. \emph{Data-free}, as used below, refers to the adapter's training data; a public G2P front-end supplies the readings, and a public automatic speech recognizer (ASR) is used as a tool where takes (sampled syntheses) are selected (below). How teachers were taken was not uniform, and this is stated. Sarashina and Irodori use ten carriers a word and keep the first take that passes the guard of \S\ref{sec:guard}, with no selection ($4{,}830$ teachers, none dropped) and no reading check; an audit after the fact (every stored teacher decoded and scored with the ASR of \S\ref{sec:exp}) hears the target reading in $0.84$ (Sarashina) and $0.89$ (Irodori) of them; $10$ and $15$ words are misread in every take, everyday words in uncommon kanji spellings read character by character, and those teachers stay in the set. CosyVoice~2 and T5Gemma use four carriers a word and keep the

($50$ of $1{,}892$ takes dropped, leaving $1{,}842$ teachers over $472$ words); of two on T5Gemma, rejected above $0.35$, where the base read more than
half the carriers too badly for any take to pass ($1{,}068$ of $1{,}932$ dropped, leaving $864$ teachers over $427$ of the $483$ words). Selection acts on training data only. T5Gemma's adapter is thus trained on what an untuned recipe left it, and its results are that recipe's floor on that backbone, not its ceiling.

\subsection{The text set, and why odaka shapes it}
The word inventory contains 533 words $\x$ 10 carriers, balanced over ten semantic domains, over mora-initial consonant rows, and over all four accent types. One type dictates the design: for \emph{odaka} words, the fall occurs on the \emph{following} particle, so it is inaudible in isolation. Every odaka carrier therefore places a particle immediately after the target, and odaka, the hardest type, is deliberately over-sampled ($15\%$); because common odaka nouns are scarce, a tenth domain (body and person terms), where they are frequent, was added to supply them. Words colliding with any target of the difficult, katakana, or Joyo evaluation sets, whether by surface or by canonicalized reading, are dropped (50 of 533), so the training and evaluation vocabularies are disjoint by construction. The CosyVoice~2 teacher script also excluded the naturalness set's targets ($10$ more words); the other three did not, so the naturalness pairs that edit one of those words are excluded (\S\ref{sec:nat}).

\textbf{Item sets.} Three sets are used. The $50$-word \emph{difficult} set is the listening set. Its ASR reading scores were observed during development, so no reading score is reported; its accent results could not have been tuned to, because no accent judgment existed before the listening study. A $50$-word \emph{easy} set per backbone, words whose reading the base already produces, serves the naturalness study alone (\S\ref{sec:nat}). The second set is drawn from the Joyo Kanji Yomi Benchmark~\cite{joyo2026}, $13{,}095$ native-verified sentences in which one kanji's reading is marked: we keep every sentence on which a public dictionary G2P (pyopenjtalk~\cite{pyopenjtalk}) reads the marked span \emph{wrongly}, drop any whose target word or reading occurs in the training inventory, and verify each remaining substitution by reading the substituted sentence back through the G2P against the benchmark's own pronunciation. Nothing about our models enters the selection, and no sampling is involved: the set is every item that passes, $424$ in all. One of four CosyVoice~2 adapters must be chosen (\S\ref{sec:reftab}), and choosing it on the reported items would be selection on the test set, so the $424$ items are split \emph{before any adapter is measured} into a $105$-item selection half and a $319$-item test half by connected component of the (word, reading) graph, so that no word or reading crosses.

Against no edit, the tag gains $+0.310$, $+0.470$, $+0.251$, and $+0.354$ on the four backbones, with every interval well clear of zero ($p<10^{-12}$ throughout): the channel reaches words it never saw tagged in every paradigm. Against plain kana, it reads $0.069$--$0.091$ lower on three of the four ($p \le 0.003$), one word in eleven to fourteen, which \S\ref{sec:conclusion} names as the open problem, and is indistinguishable on Sarashina ($-0.022$, $[-0.074,+0.033]$).

Voice matters: over the $150$ pairs of test items sharing a word and reading under different voices, renditions disagree more often under the tag than with no edit on all four backbones (Sarashina $26.0\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$, CosyVoice~2 $28.7\%$ vs.\ $14.0\%$, Irodori $18.0\%$ vs.\ $13.3\%$, T5Gemma $29.3\%$ vs.\ $22.0\%$).

SpeechSplice~\cite{kurihara2026speechsplice}, concurrent work, edits pronunciation on T5Gemma-TTS with no training by replacing encoder hidden states; the present method needs no such intervention point.

One cause is visible in how a teacher is produced. Sarashina emits semantic tokens from text alone, so its teachers carry no speaker. CosyVoice~2 cannot emit audio without a reference clip, so every teacher is spoken in some voice, and the prompt speaker is baked into the target's pronunciation. Table~\ref{tab:dose} varies only the number of synthetic teacher voices, on the selection half under two references used for this choice alone. The choice is a worst case over references, so it uses two clean ones rather than many: ITA-corpus~\cite{oguchi2021ita} studio recordings, one female (A = amitaro) and one male (B = kamijou), held out from every training and teacher stage and from JSUT/JVS, so a drop under either is the adapter's, not the clip's.


Diversity is necessary but saturates: one voice to five lifts reference A from $0.54$ to $0.68$ ($p=0.020$), while twenty buy nothing over five ($p=0.33$, $1.00$). The five-voice adapter was chosen by a rule fixed before the numbers existed, the higher of the two references as the minimum, and is used throughout.

Accent realization is a correctness judgment, so ability is gated by a known-answer screening test rather than by credentials. Admission requires $18$ of $19$ known-answer items, a threshold fixed before recruitment; the first attempt is binding. Candidates work with Japanese pitch accent, either professionally or in training; every recruitment route takes the same test, every candidate is paid according to their score, and no rater is told which rendition comes from which system.

Each admitted rater judges all $473$ stimuli plus eight known-answer catch trials. Fleiss' $\kappa$ is reported \emph{before} any system comparison; the bootstrap resamples words and raters; duplicate items give within-rater consistency, and a rater below $6/8$ on the catch trials is excluded and reported. Three contrasts are confirmatory (McNemar exact, Holm-corrected): the edit against no edit on Sarashina2.2-TTS and on Irodori, and on Sarashina, the edit against \emph{kana input}, the contrast on which the method's value rests (\S\ref{sec:kana}). The design and analysis were fixed before any audio was heard. The stimulus and screening definitions, the evaluation scripts, the text set, the teacher sets, the adapter weights (under each backbone's license), and the training code are released.

\textbf{Results.} Thirty-two candidates were screened ($16$ from an open call, $15$ by individual contract, $1$ by direct approach) and five passed ($2$, $2$, $1$); one could not be reached, so four raters were admitted, all sessions complete. Fleiss' $\kappa$ on the binary outcome (prescribed accent realized or not), over the $448$ stimuli left after excluding duplicates and ``cannot judge'' answers, is $0.85$, pairwise Cohen's $\kappa$ $0.83$--$0.87$; catch-trial scores are $6$--$8$ of $8$ and duplicate consistency at least $22/23$, so no rater is excluded; $4$ tied items are excluded. On Sarashina, the tag realizes the prescribed accent on $0.89$ of words against $0.57$ for kana input (risk difference $+0.32$ $[+0.19,+0.45]$, Holm $p=2\times10^{-4}$), and kana wins no pair (discordant $0$ vs.\ $15$); against no edit it is $0.88$ vs.\ $0.66$ ($+0.22$ $[+0.06,+0.38]$, Holm $p=0.038$). gain is reading: no edit draws $61$ reading and $9$ accent failure judgments, the tag $1$ and $26$, and with reading failures removed, the two are level ($0.89$ vs.\ $0.94$, $p=0.69$). Over kana, the gain is accent alone. On Irodori, the tag and no edit tie at $0.78$ ($+0.00$ $[-0.16,+0.16]$). Editing a \emph{different} word in the sentence moves the judged word's accent from $1.00$ to $0.94$ ($[-0.14,0.00]$). On CosyVoice~2, the data-free adapter realizes the accent on $0.66$ of words against $0.96$ for the adapter trained on $15{,}097$ recorded pairs ($-0.30$ $[-0.44,-0.16]$).

\textbf{Results} ($86$ sittings, $76$ complete, $3{,}228$ judgments on $168$ pairs, $15$--$22$ per pair). Excluded are one account's second sitting, three sittings answered faster than the clips could be played (median interval under $4.7$\,s), and the $29$ pairs whose edited word was in that backbone's training inventory ($10$, $10$ and $9$ on Sarashina, Irodori and T5Gemma; \S\ref{sec:method}). With ties split evenly, the share preferring the unedited rendition minus the share preferring the edited one is $-0.08$ $[-0.24,+0.08]$ on Sarashina and $+0.43$ $[+0.31,+0.56]$ on Irodori, $+0.33$ $[+0.19,+0.46]$ on CosyVoice~2 and $+0.30$ $[+0.11,+0.48]$ on T5Gemma. The registered non-inferiority margin of $0.15$ is met on Sarashina, the backbone on which the recipe was developed, and on none of the three was it moved to untuned. The $127$ pairs in which both renditions yield the same reading give the same picture ($-0.07$, $+0.41$, $+0.36$, $+0.34$): the cost lies in how the word is said, not in which word.
